name: System Architecture Diagram
description: The inventory browser interface sends authenticated JSON requests to Express. Inventory services validate stock operations and persist related records through Sequelize in MySQL.
note: Vite is the development server/build tool. Prepared stock is stored on MenuItem, not in a separate prepared-stock table. This diagram refines the user-supplied first-version reference.

name: Class Diagram
description: This class diagram shows the receiving model relationships and the supporting inventory classes, with selected attributes and actual service functions. Stock quantities use decimals for supplies and integers for prepared menu stock.
note: Multiplicity is shown on the principal associations; supporting references remain typed attributes to preserve readability. StockCount/WasteReport link to StockItem and StockBatch; MenuRecipe links to MenuItem; StockAllocation links to Order. User audit references are shown without expanding user management. Service functions are module operations, not invented model methods.

name: Component Diagram
description: Inventory screens depend on the shared inventory data provider and HTTP client. The Express router uses access checks, domain services and Sequelize persistence; order integration remains an external inventory boundary.
note: These are logical software components within one frontend and one backend application. No microservice deployment or independent API gateway is implemented.

name: Deployment Diagram
description: The deployment diagram maps the inventory artifacts to the local browser, Node.js runtime and MySQL service. The configured development ports are 5173 for Vite, 3000 for Express and 3306 for MySQL.
note: This is the configured local topology, not a fresh observation of running processes. render.yaml is a backend hosting configuration; live hosting, cloud networking, load balancing and backups are not verified.

name: Object Diagram
description: This object diagram instantiates the receiving classes after one example receipt. Underlined instance names, attribute slots and solid links show a consistent snapshot of supplier, item, batch, receipt, line and movement objects.
note: All IDs, names, dates and values are illustrative. They describe a valid implemented operation and do not claim these records exist in the business database.

name: Package Diagram
description: The package diagram groups inventory source files by their actual frontend and backend directories. It shows the dependency path from inventory screens to the HTTP client, backend routes, services and models.
note: Packages are documentation groupings of JavaScript/TypeScript directories, not separately deployable services. Shared code is included only where inventory depends on it.

name: Composite Structure Diagram
description: The composite structure diagram opens the inventory router boundary to show its collaborating middleware, route handler, stock service and Sequelize model parts. Ports represent the HTTP request boundary and SQL persistence boundary.
note: The implementation uses modules, functions and an Express Router object. This UML structured classifier is a documentation abstraction, not an additional runtime inventory class.

name: Profile Diagram
description: This profile defines three inventory-specific UML stereotypes for records, service components and stock operations. Each stereotype extends the appropriate UML metaclass and supplies concise documentation tags.
note: No UML profile is implemented or loaded by the application. This newly defined documentation profile fulfills the activity table without claiming a runtime feature or industry certification.

name: Data Flow Diagram (DFD)
description: This level 1 DFD follows stock receiving data from an authorized actor through authentication, receipt processing and presentation. It includes user records, duplicate-request records and the stock persistence data store.
note: D3 groups actual inventory tables, including suppliers; it is not a new database table. The browser subsequently reads updated balances. DFD arrows carry data and do not imply transaction control order.

name: Use Case Diagram
description: This use case diagram shows the inventory goals available to Inventory Staff and Admin, including the Admin-only count review, reversal and policy controls. Cashier and Kitchen actors appear only for relevant read access and Kitchen waste reporting.
note: Authentication is a precondition for all use cases. The Admin actor generalization represents shared inventory capabilities, not a role inheritance mechanism in the code. Count approval policy and adjustment limits are Admin-controlled; ordinary Inventory settings remain editable by Inventory Staff.

name: Activity Diagram
description: The activity diagram shows a stock receipt from submission through access checks, request identity handling, unit conversion and transactional persistence. Identical retries return the saved result; failed operations roll back.
note: Exception connectors summarize failure exits from transaction actions. A correction resubmits through the form; the next refresh reads balances rather than retrying a failed save automatically.

name: Sequence Diagram
description: This sequence follows a successful new receiving request through the UI, Express inventory handler and Sequelize/MySQL persistence. The related receipt, batches, balance changes, movements and operation result commit together.
note: Router and stock service share a lifeline for readability; Sequelize and MySQL also share a persistence lifeline. Return arrows are dashed. Identical retries and rollback are documented alternatives to this main scenario.

name: State Machine Diagram
description: The state machine models the four implemented StockCount status values. A valid count is immediately applied or placed in pending review; Admin review applies, rejects or marks it stale if the balance version or reserved quantity makes it unsafe.
note: The initial decision occurs before record creation and depends on actor role, countApproval and adjustmentLimit. A stale record stays historical; recounting creates a new record. No automatic review timer exists.

name: Communication Diagram
description: This communication diagram uses the same receiving scenario as the sequence diagram, emphasizing the network of collaborating objects. Hierarchical message numbers identify the request, service call, transactional operations and replies.
note: Access middleware is summarized in the router interaction; it loads the approved user before the service runs. The transaction alternatives are the same as in Diagrams 11 and 12.

name: Interaction Overview Diagram
description: The interaction overview connects receiving authorization, the detailed stock transaction and inventory readback as referenced interactions. Decisions route denied access and failed transactions to their corresponding UI outcomes.
note: The stock transaction interaction is expanded in Diagram 12. Failure paths end the current attempt; a corrected submission begins a new interaction. No parallel background save is implied.

name: Timing Diagram
description: This timing diagram shows the visible-tab state and refresh/request states across the configured 30-second polling ticks. The initial refresh and subsequent successful requests update the inventory data and timestamp.
note: The illustrated 3- and 4-second request durations are examples only. setInterval is a schedule, not a deadline guarantee; hidden tabs skip interval-triggered requests, focus/manual refresh can run earlier, and older responses are ignored using a sequence counter. No real-time push or hard latency guarantee is implemented.

name: Requirement Diagram (SysML)
description: The requirement diagram expresses five concrete inventory rules supported by the implementation and links each rule to the code element that satisfies it. SysML requirement blocks carry an ID and requirement text; satisfy arrows point to the requirement.
note: These are implementation-derived documentation requirements. No independent client requirement baseline, formal SysML model or real-time performance requirement was supplied. Test code was inspected for corresponding scenarios; this document does not claim a fresh test execution.
